definitions: On(0,L), take finitely many distinct interior x_j andα_j≥0. On H₀¹ define q[u]=∫|u′|²dx+Σα_j|u(x_j)|².
The associated operator acts as−u″ between interaction points. Its domain has u continuous, piecewise H², Dirichlet endpoints and jumps u′(x_j+)−u′(x_j−)=α_ju(x_j).

result.name: A closed positive form, spectral bracket and conditional perturbation derivative
result.statement: The form defines a positive self-adjoint operator with discrete spectrum. With r interaction points, (nπ/L)²≤λ_n≤((n+r)π/L)², henceλ_n=(nπ/L)²+O(n). For a differentiable simple eigenbranch of q_ε=q₀+εΣα_j|u(x_j)|², λ_n′(0)=(2/L)Σα_j sin²(nπx_j/L).
result.proof: Point evaluation is continuous on H₀¹, for example|u(x)|≤√L||u′||₂. Thus the form norm is equivalent to the H₀¹ norm and is closed; the closed-form representation theorem and compact embedding into L² are the stated classical functional-analytic inputs. Integration by parts on each subinterval gives the jump conditions. The lower bound is min–max monotonicity. For the upper bound, intersect the span of the first n+r free sine modes with the r evaluation kernels; its dimension is at least n, and on it the interaction term vanishes, giving the bound. For the derivative formula, differentiate the normalized eigenvalue identity; the terms from differentiating the eigenvector cancel by the eigen-equation and normalization, leaving the form derivative evaluated on√(2/L)sin(nπx/L).

example.calculation: A symmetric ground mode has wavenumber k∈(1,3/2) satisfying2k cot(πk/2)+2=0. The endpoint signs are exactly positive at1 and negative at3/2, and monotonicity gives one root; λ=k² lies in(1,9/4). Antisymmetric free modes vanishing at the midpoint remain unchanged. entries.title: A fibre functor reconstructs a finite group only with its whole category
entries.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
entries.summary: Grothendieck’s Galois theory is a substantial theorem about categories and fibre functors. A finite group version admits a short complete proof and identifies the essential naturality requirement. It does not assert that the historical modal implementation exists.
definitions: Let G be a finite group, FinGSet its category of finite left G-sets and equivariant maps, and F its forgetful functor to finite sets.
A natural automorphismη of F is a family of bijectionsη_X:F(X)→F(X) commuting with every equivariant map. Its components are not required to be equivariant themselves.

result.name: Aut(F) is canonically G
result.statement: The map a∈G↦[η_X(x)=ax] is a group isomorphism G→Aut(F). Natural automorphisms are determined by their action on the identity element of the regular G-set.
result.proof: For any a, equivariance of a map f gives f(ax)=af(x), so the family is natural; the inverse family uses a^(−1). Conversely letη be natural and let a=η_G(1), where G carries its left regular action. For any G-set X and x∈X, the map f_x:G→X, g↦gx, is equivariant. Naturality givesη_X(x)=η_X(f_x(1))=f_x(η_G(1))=ax. Thus every natural family has the displayed form and its a is unique. Composition of families corresponds to multiplication ab, proving the group law. The proof uses all these maps f_x; isolated orbit sizes or a single matrix do not supply the reconstruction.

example.setup: Take G=C₃ acting regularly on{0,1,2} by cyclic addition.
example.calculation: The three possible natural families restrict to the three cyclic shifts on the regular set. A transposition fails to commute with its equivariant right translations and therefore cannot be a natural automorphism. The verifier enumerates all six permutations and retains exactly three.
example.conclusion: The finite model shows what is reconstructed and why categorical compatibility is mathematical data rather than a label.

definitions: Work over R with a finite-dimensional representation of C₂, specified by S²=I. Let V_+=ker(S−I) and V_−=ker(S+I), with projections P_±=(I±S)/2.

entries.title: Projective motivic cohomology retains the base field in every summand
entries.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
entries.summary: Several retrieved rules attempted to compute all motivic cohomology from a small inequality in p,q,n. The projective-bundle theorem instead shifts the motivic cohomology of the base field. On the Chow diagonal this simplifies beautifully, but it does not erase off-diagonal field information.
definitions: For a field k and standard integral motivic cohomology of smooth schemes, use H^{p,q}(X,Z)=CH^q(X,2q−p).
Let h be the hyperplane class of bidegree(2,1). The classical projective-bundle theorem is the stated input below.

result.name: Correct projective decomposition and the Chow diagonal
result.statement: H^{p,q}(P^n_k,Z)≅⊕_{i=0}^n H^{p−2i,q−i}(Spec k,Z). In particular CH^*(P^n_k)=Z[h]/(h^{n+1}); hence H^{2q,q}=Z for0≤q≤n and zero outside that Chow range. Other bidegrees are not specified by that diagonal rule.
result.proof: The projective-bundle theorem states thatΣh^iπ^* gives the displayed isomorphism, withπ:P^n→Spec k. The shifts follow from deg(h^i)=(2i,i). On the diagonal, H^{2r,r}(k)=CH^r(Spec k), which is Z for r=0 and zero for r>0 because a point has no positive-codimension cycles. Thus only i=q survives, yielding the polynomial Chow ring and the relation h^{n+1}=0. Off the diagonal, H^{1,1}(k)=k× is generally nonzero, so a computer rule returning merely zero or one Tate symbol loses genuine base-field data. The general projective-bundle theorem is cited rather than claimed as proved by finite tests; the diagonal and grading consequences are derived explicitly.

example.setup: For P² compute its Chow ranks and the product h·h.
example.calculation: The groups in bidegrees(0,0),(2,1),(4,2) are each Z, h² is the point class, and h³=0. For P¹, H^{1,1} contains k× even though its Chow ranks are only one in codimensions zero and one. entries.title: A strong correlation is not a causal policy proof
entries.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
entries.summary: The source’s assistant called a transportation analysis a mathematical proof and treated correlations as causal certainty. definitions: Let U,V be independent mean-zero, variance-one variables. Define X=U and Y=−U+σV. An intervention do(X=x) replaces only the equation for X.
For a stipulated constant annual quantity b, discount r>0, horizon N and initial quantity C in compatible units, define V_N=Σ_{t=1}^N b/(1+r)^t−C.

result.name: An exact confounding example and a geometric-sum formula
result.statement: Corr(X,Y)=−1/√(1+σ²), yet do(X=x) leaves the distribution of Y unchanged. Choosingσ²=(1000/973)²−1 gives correlation−.973 exactly. Also V_N=b[1−(1+r)^(−N)]/r−C.
result.proof: Cov(X,Y)=−Var(U)=−1, Var(X)=1 and Var(Y)=1+σ², proving the correlation. The equation for Y contains U,V but no X, so intervening on X does not change it. Observational association can therefore be arbitrarily close to−1 with zero causal effect. For the sum, set a=(1+r)^(−1); Σ_{t=1}^Na^t=a(1−a^N)/(1−a)=[1−(1+r)^(−N)]/r. entries.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
entries.summary: The g-dyad proposal gives an explicit nonlinear action. Its derivative and compositions can be developed without claiming that arbitrary nonlinear or hysteretic behavior is a tensor product. A conservative-field test also determines when the action can come from a scalar variational energy.
definitions: Let a,b∈R^d be fixed nonzero vectors and f:R→R be C¹. Define F(x)=a f(bᵀx). For composition let G(x)=c g(dᵀx).

result.name: Derivative, composition and a potential criterion
result.statement: DF(x)=f′(bᵀx)abᵀ has rank at most one. F∘G(x)=a f((bᵀc)g(dᵀx)). If f′ is nonzero somewhere, F is a gradient field on R^d exactly when a is parallel to b.
result.proof: Apply the chain rule componentwise to obtain the Jacobian and its rank bound. Substitution gives the composition, which generally leaves the original activation family unless it is closed under this scalar nesting. If F=∇V with V C², its Jacobian is symmetric, so abᵀ=baᵀ wherever f′≠0. For nonzero a,b this equality implies linear dependence: apply both sides to b to get a||b||²=b(a·b). Conversely if a=κb and F₀′=f, then V(x)=κF₀(bᵀx) has gradientκbf(bᵀx)=F(x). Thus a variational energy exists under an explicit alignment condition, not for every chosen dyad. For f(s)=s the composition reduces to the familiar rank-one matrix identity(abᵀ)(cdᵀ)=(bᵀc)adᵀ.

example.calculation: F(x,y)=(y²,0), with Jacobian[[0,2y],[0,0]]. At y≠0 it is nonsymmetric, so it cannot be the gradient of a C² potential. Choosing instead a=b=(1,0) gives F=(x²,0)=∇(x³/3). The verifier checks the derivative matrices, rank and linear composition identity exactly.

entries.title: Nonlocal dyad learning needs an adjoint in its variational update
entries.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
entries.summary: The source’s reconstruction and regularization terms are specific enough to motivate a rigorous linear inverse problem. Its update uses the adjoint of the forward operator, not the operator itself unless self-adjointness has been proved. Positivity then supplies a uniqueness certificate.
definitions: Let K:H→Y be a bounded linear map between real Hilbert spaces. In a finite-dimensional model define J(u)=||Ku−y||²/2+α||u||²/2 withα>0.
For a smooth field on a bounded domain, addβ∫|∇u|²/2 withβ≥0 and choose boundary conditions before integration by parts.

result.name: A coercive normal equation and its gradient
result.statement: The finite model has unique minimizer(K* K+αI)u=K*y. With an H¹ term its formal Euler equation is K*(Ku−y)+αu−βΔu=0, with the chosen natural or fixed boundary conditions.
result.proof: Differentiate J(u+εv) at zero to obtain⟨Ku−y,Kv⟩+α⟨u,v⟩=⟨K*(Ku−y)+αu,v⟩. Thus the derivative vanishes for every v exactly at the normal equation. The quadratic form of K*K+αI is||Kv||²+α||v||²≥α||v||², so the finite matrix is positive definite and invertible, proving existence and uniqueness. For the gradient term, integration by parts givesβ∫∇u·∇v=−β∫Δu v plus boundary flux; it vanishes for fixed variations or yields a Neumann condition in the natural problem. In infinite dimensions a corresponding coercive bilinear-form theorem supplies existence under stated domain assumptions, rather than a matrix inverse being assumed automatically.

example.conclusion: The adjoint, coercivity constant and objective gap can all be verified independently of the proposed learning architecture.

entries.limits: Optimizing activation parameters or enforcing nonlinear spectral constraints generally destroys this convexity. A CP tensor factorization has scaling ambiguities and is not unique merely because a reconstruction error is small.

entries.title: Exhaustive finite tests prove a polynomial identity only with a degree bound
entries.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
entries.summary: The source correctly distinguished computational verification from deductive proof. A finite-field identity theorem makes that distinction sharper: an exhaustive test can be a complete certificate within a specified reduced polynomial space. Without the degree restriction a nonzero polynomial can vanish at every test point.
definitions: Let f∈F₃[x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄] have degree at most two in each separate variable. Evaluate it on every point of F₃⁴.
The polynomial-function quotient is F₃[x₁,…,x₄]/(x₁³−x₁,…,x₄³−x₄). Each class has a unique representative with those separate degree bounds.

result.name: A complete finite certificate and its exact counterexample
result.statement: If the reduced f vanishes on all81 points, then f is the zero polynomial. Without the bound, x₁³−x₁ is a nonzero formal polynomial that vanishes at all81 points.
result.proof: A univariate polynomial of degree at most two over a field with three distinct roots is zero. View f as a polynomial in x₄ with coefficients in the first three variables. For any fixed values of those three variables, its three x₄ evaluations force all three coefficients to vanish at that triple. Repeat the argument in the remaining variables; induction makes every coefficient zero. Existence of a reduced representative follows by repeatedly replacing x_i³ by x_i, lowering degree; uniqueness follows from the just-proved evaluation injectivity. There are3^81 reduced polynomials and3^81 functions on an81-point set, so evaluation is also surjective. The counterexample violates the degree restriction and is zero only in the quotient of polynomial functions.

example.setup: Test the identity(x+y)³=x³+y³ over F₃ and distinguish it from the formal claim x³=x.
example.calculation: The first is a true polynomial identity because intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by three. The second is true as a function on F₃ but false in the polynomial ring. The verifier evaluates every point and independently compares coefficient dictionaries, showing both the complete bounded certificate and the danger of an unstated quotient.
example.conclusion: A program can issue a deductive finite certificate when its theorem class and algebra are explicit.

entries.limits: Testing a finite domain does not prove arbitrary integer, real, analytic or number-theoretic conjectures. The recovered program description does not provide its actual proof certificates, source code or a formal soundness theorem.
entries.extension: Have the research engine emit a reduced polynomial, the reduction trace and all evaluation values, then check that certificate with a small independent verifier. General conjecture generation should remain separate from the trusted proof kernel.

entries.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
entries.summary: The program description names B₄,E₆,E₇,E₈ and coordinate reflections. Signed coordinate permutations give a genuine B₄ action with an exact finite classification. definitions: Let B₄ be the group of signed4×4 permutation matrices over F₃. Each sign is±1, distinct in this field. It acts on the81 vectors in F₃⁴.
Hamming weight w(x) is the number of nonzero coordinates. The reduced quadratic sumΣx_i² equals w(x) modulo three, a coarser invariant.

result.name: Order, orbits and a faithful-representation obstruction
result.statement: |B₄|=2⁴·4!=384. Its orbits are exactly the five Hamming-weight classes, of sizes1,8,24,32,16. A faithful linear action of W(E₈) on F₃⁴ is impossible because|W(E₈)|=696729600 exceeds|GL₄(F₃)|=24261120.
result.proof: Choose a permutation of the four coordinates and an independent sign for each output coordinate; the resulting384 matrices are distinct. They preserve the number of nonzero coordinates. Conversely any vector of weight r can be moved to(1,…,1,0,…,0) by a permutation and sign flips, proving one orbit for each r. Choose its support in binomial(4,r) ways and its nonzero signs in2^r ways, giving the sizes. Their sum is81. For the obstruction, a faithful linear action embeds its group into GL₄(F₃). Counting ordered independent columns gives(81−1)(81−3)(81−9)(81−27)=24261120, too small for W(E₈). The quoted E₈ order is a classical root-system input; the cardinality contradiction is elementary.

example.calculation: Both have quadratic sum one modulo three, but their Hamming weights one and four put them in different B₄ orbits. The verifier enumerates all81 vectors and all384 signed permutations, checking the orbit partition exactly. It also checks the GL order and the order obstruction.
example.conclusion: A complete finite group-action result replaces a loose exceptional-group label without claiming a review of unrecovered source code.

entries.title: A SAT avoidance complex does not make all 2-SAT instances contractible
entries.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
entries.summary: The early July project proposed a homological complexity hierarchy. Its simplicial construction can be made coherent, but its asserted topological classification needs independent proof. Even the empty2-CNF formula provides a decisive counterexample to universal contractibility.
definitions: For n Boolean variables use vertices x_i,¬x_i. A face contains no opposite pair and no set consisting of all negated literals of a clause. A full face chooses exactly one literal per variable; it represents the corresponding truth assignment. Reduced homology uses an explicitly chosen coefficient field.

result.name: Satisfying facets and a counterexample
result.statement: Full(n−1)-dimensional faces correspond exactly to satisfying assignments. With no clauses, the complex is the join of n two-point sets, the boundary of the n-dimensional crosspolytope, homeomorphic to S^(n−1). It is not contractible for n≥1.
result.proof: A full face satisfies a clause precisely when it does not choose all the clause’s negations. Applying that test to every clause proves the assignment correspondence. With no clauses, only opposite-pair exclusions remain. Each variable contributes a choice of either endpoint of a0-sphere, and joining these choices gives the crosspolytope boundary. Its reduced homology in degree n−1 is one-dimensional. The formula with no clauses is a valid2-CNF formula and is trivially satisfiable, yet has nontrivial topology. Therefore neither satisfiability nor ease of decision implies contractibility for this construction. An entropy or Betti profile may still be studied as an observable, but cannot inherit a complexity theorem from its name.

example.setup: Use two variables and no clauses.
example.calculation: The vertices x,¬x,y,¬y form a four-cycle with edges joining choices from different variables. It has four vertices,four edges and no triangles, so β₁=1. Adding suitable clauses can delete faces and change the topology without establishing a monotone decision-complexity scale.

result.proof: If one basket costs P0 initially and PT=P0(1+pi)^T later, a fixed nominal amount buys PT/P0 times fewer baskets; its relative purchasing power is P0/PT. entries.title: A Mellin split gives a reproducible central L-value formula
entries.status: Developed classical result with a scoped worked example
entries.summary: The historical approximate-functional-equation outputs disagree even in sign. For a weight-two form, splitting the Mellin integral at the Fricke fixed point gives a rapidly convergent center formula whose normalization can be checked directly.
definitions: Let f(tau)=sum(n>=1)a_n exp(2pi*i*n*tau) be a weight-two cusp form of level N.
Assume f(i/(N*t))=epsilon*N*t²*f(i*t), epsilon=+1 or -1, and |a_n|<=2n. Put c=2pi/sqrt(N).

result.name: Exact central-value series with an explicit tail
result.statement: L(1,f)=(1+epsilon)sum(n>=1)(a_n/n)exp(-c*n). Truncation after M terms has absolute tail at most2|1+epsilon|exp[-c(M+1)]/(1-exp(-c)).
result.proof: The Mellin identity gives L(1,f)=2pi integral(0,infinity)f(i*t)dt. Set A=1/sqrt(N) and substitute t=1/(N*u) in the lower integral. The Fricke identity turns it into epsilon integral(A,infinity)f(i*u)du. Thus the full integral equals(1+epsilon) times the upper integral. Termwise integration is justified by absolute exponential convergence on t>=A and gives the stated series. The coefficient bound yields |a_n/n|<=2, so a geometric series bounds the omitted tail. In particular epsilon=-1 forces the center value to vanish. For an elliptic newform, the bound follows from |a_n|<=d(n)sqrt(n) and the elementary inequality d(n)<=2sqrt(n).

example.setup: For N=11 use f=eta(tau)²eta(11*tau)², whose Fricke sign is epsilon=+1.
example.calculation: The q product q*product(1-q^n)²(1-q^(11n))² yields exact integer coefficients. Twenty terms give approximately0.2538418608559107, with analytic tail below3e-17 under the coefficient bound. The numerical approximation has its own rounding error; the tail formula is independent of quadrature-node choices.
example.conclusion: The local normalization, functional equation and truncation error are exposed rather than hidden in a generic AFE routine.

entries.limits: The theorem assumes genuine modular coefficients and the stated Fricke law. Applying it to arbitrary surrogate traces would not construct a modular L-function.
entries.extension: Implement interval exponential evaluation and retain the exact Fourier coefficients plus the analytic tail to produce a completely rounded central-value enclosure.

entries.title: Cubic KKT equations do not certify a global maximum
entries.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
entries.summary: The August9 maximality solver repeatedly produced KKT roots and square-root formulas. Their algebra is a necessary first-order condition under regularity, not an automatic global certificate. A one-dimensional cubic constraint makes both sign branches and missing optima explicit.
definitions: Consider f(x)=cᵀx and equality constraints g_i(x)=Σ_jA_ijx_j³−b_i=0. With L=f+Σλ_ig_i, set S_j=Σ_iλ_iA_ij. Assume the constraint gradients are independent at the candidate.

result.statement: A regular constrained extremum satisfies c_j+3x_j²S_j=0. If S_j≠0, real solutions require−c_j/(3S_j)≥0 and generally have both signs. Stationarity alone implies neither existence nor global optimality.

Finally a continuous objective reaches a maximum on a nonempty compact feasible set, but arbitrary affine algebraic sets need not be compact; a cubic parametrization does not supply boundedness.

entries.title: Consistent Gaussian coordinates need not live in the Hilbert space
entries.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
entries.summary: The August9 synthesis invoked Sazonov and Minlos. A diagonal Hilbert-space construction proves a concrete sufficient condition and exhibits the failure of identity covariance. This keeps a genuine measure theorem separate from formal consistency or category names.
definitions: Let H=ℓ² with basis e_n and independent standard normals Z_n. For q_n≥0 consider X=Σ√q_nZ_ne_n. The covariance has diagonal entries q_n.

result.name: Trace-summable construction and identity-covariance failure
result.statement: IfΣq_n<∞, X converges almost surely in H and in mean square, with characteristic function exp(−Σq_nh_n²/2). For q_n=1 the coordinate law givesℓ² probability zero.
result.proof: The nonnegative random sum S=Σq_nZ_n² has expectationΣq_n by monotone convergence. Finite expectation implies S<∞ almost surely, which is exactly square summability of the coordinates. The tail mean-square error equalsΣ_{n>N}q_n, proving L² convergence. Finite Gaussian characteristic functions multiply, and dominated convergence yields the displayed limit. The resulting Borel probability on the Polish spaceℓ² is Radon. By contrast the strong law gives N⁻¹Σ_{n≤N}Z_n²→1 almost surely when q_n=1, forcing divergence of the squared norm. Consistency of all finite marginals remains true, but their product measure is supported outsideℓ².

example.setup: Choose q_n=2^(−n),n≥1.
example.calculation: The covariance trace and E||X||² are one. Truncation after N has squared mean error2^(−N). Identity-covariance truncations have expected squared norm N and their probability of lying in any fixed-radius ball tends to zero.
example.conclusion: Support and tightness, not just finite consistency, are the decisive missing hypotheses.

entries.limits: This proves the diagonal case, not the general Sazonov or nuclear-space Minlos theorem. Cameron–Martin vectors and typical samples also have different meanings.
entries.extension: Specify the actual topological vector space and covariance, then prove the continuity/tightness assumptions of the chosen extension theorem.

definitions: Let Mr=λr,ℓᵀM=λℓᵀ,ℓᵀr=1 and Π=rℓᵀ. Assume λ is simple and all other eigenvalues have modulus belowλ>0.

result.name: Correct spectral projection decomposition

Powers of R/λ tend to zero in finite dimension when its spectral radius is below one, including possible polynomial Jordan factors. The erroneous definition subtracts only r from Mr, leaving(λ−1)r, which directly contradicts the claimed annihilation unlessλ=1. Also a number1−ρ(R) is not a universal transient norm budget for a nonnormal matrix.

entries.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
entries.summary: The August23 testbeds named Ramanujan graphs, graph zeta functions and primitive geodesics. A finite incidence construction gives a complete spectral certificate. It distinguishes the ordinary Laplacian zeta from Ihara’s nonbacktracking zeta.
definitions: Let B be the7×7 point-line incidence matrix of the Fano plane: each point lies on three lines and each distinct pair shares one line. Let A=[[0,B],[Bᵀ,0]] and L=3I−A. Remove the zero Laplacian eigenvalue from ζ_L(s).

result.name: Exact Heawood spectrum and zeta
result.statement: A has eigenvalues3,−3, and±√2 each with multiplicity six. Thus ζ_L(s)=6(3−√2)^(−s)+6(3+√2)^(−s)+6^(−s).
result.proof: The incidence property gives BBᵀ=2I+J. On the constant line this has eigenvalue9, while the six-dimensional orthogonal complement has eigenvalue2. The symmetric block adjacency matrix therefore has the positive and negative singular values3 and√2 with the stated multiplicities. Subtracting from3 gives Laplacian eigenvalues0,6,3±√2. Their power sum proves the zeta formula. The nontrivial adjacency values satisfy the cubic Ramanujan bound2√(3−1), but that does not identify graph zeta zeros with arithmetic L-function zeros. Ihara’s determinant formula uses det(I−uA+2u²I) and a separate factor(1−u²)^(21−14), not the Laplacian inverse-power sum.

example.setup: Evaluate ζ_L(1).
example.calculation: The conjugate reciprocal sum is1/(3−√2)+1/(3+√2)=6/7, so ζ_L(1)=36/7+1/6=223/42. The graph has14 vertices and21 edges; its girth-six property is separately checked from its incidence structure.
example.conclusion: A complete finite operator identity supports the exact graph claims and keeps the two zeta constructions distinct.

entries.limits: This does not prove a number-field Riemann hypothesis, spectral universality or a statistical law for arbitrary graphs.

entries.summary: The historical pipeline proposed DFT derivatives for a critical-line zero hunt. Fourier differentiation can be exact and useful, provided its object is identified: it differentiates the trigonometric interpolant selected by the sample grid. Finite samples alone cannot bound derivatives of an unrestricted analytic function.
definitions: Sample a2π-periodic function at x_j=2πj/N, j=0,…,N−1. The DFT assigns coefficients to one representative of each frequency class modulo N.

result.statement: DFT differentiation exactly recovers derivatives of the declared band-limited polynomial. Without a frequency or analytic-tail bound, no finite sample grid gives a uniform derivative-error bound: h(x)=cos(Nx)−1 vanishes on the grid but h″(0)=−N².

definitions: A holomorphic function has a zero of multiplicity two at z₀ exactly when f(z₀)=f′(z₀)=0 and f″(z₀)≠0.

definitions: Let resource shares be rationals q∈[0,1]. Define q⊕r=q+r only when q+r≤1; zero is the identity.

definitions: For f∈Z_p[X], a simple root modulo p is a residue a₀ with f(a₀)≡0 modp and f′(a₀) not divisible by p.

result.name: Newton lifting supplies an exact p-adic certificate rather than a digest comparison
result.statement: If v_p(f(a))≥m≥1 and f′(a) is a unit, the Newton step has v_p(f(a′))≥2m and a′≡a modp^m. Repetition converges to the unique root in a+pZ_p. For f=X²−2,p=7, the residue3 lifts to a genuine7-adic square root.

The derivative remains a unit because a′≡a modp. The successive corrections have valuations tending to infinity, so completeness of Z_p gives a root. If two roots x,y share a modulo p, then f(x)−f(y)=(x−y)u with u a unit, by the same derivative argument; hence x=y.

entries.summary: The corrected Morphic Echo proposal replaced informal equality with a chain map and its cone. This is a precise mathematical improvement: quasi-isomorphism has an exact obstruction complex, and the identity map admits an explicit contracting homotopy.
definitions: Use cochain complexes with d increasing degree. For a cochain map f:C→D, Cone(f)ⁿ=Dⁿ⊕C^(n+1), with differential d(y,x)=(d_Dy+fx,−d_Cx).
A quasi-isomorphism induces an isomorphism on every cohomology group. A complex is contractible if dh+hd is its identity for some degree−1 map h.

result.statement: Cone(id_C) is contractible by h(y,x)=(0,y). More generally Cone(f) is acyclic if and only if f is a quasi-isomorphism.
result.proof: The cone differential squares to zero because d_Df=fd_C: its first component has the two cross terms cancel, while the second is d_C²x. For f=id, dh(y,x)=(y,−dy) and hd(y,x)=(0,dy+x); their sum is(y,x). Contractibility forces cohomology to vanish because every closed v equals d(hv). For general f, the short exact sequence0→D→Cone(f)→C[1]→0 gives a long exact cohomology sequence whose connecting map is H(f). Exactness shows that vanishing cone cohomology is equivalent to H(f) being injective and surjective in every degree. This classical exact-sequence input is stated explicitly.

Over Z the same cone has cokernel Z/2, so it is not acyclic. The coefficient ring changes the certificate even though the displayed matrix is unchanged.

entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The sealing proposal invoked a pushout and verifier replay. A finite vector-space pushout provides an actual mathematical model: it glues two interfaces along their shared part. Its universal property expresses compatibility independently of file names, hashes or motives.
definitions: For maps i:A→B and j:A→C over Q, define P=(B⊕C)/{(i(a),−j(a)):a∈A}.

Every quotient class is a sum of an image from B and one from C, so these composites determine w uniquely. For injective i and j, the relation subspace is an injected copy of A; subtracting its dimension gives the formula.

entries.title: A regulator is a Gram determinant tied to a generator basis
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The reported narrow regulator interval is meaningful only after fixing the points, height convention and error bounds. A positive-definite lattice model gives the exact change-of-basis law and shows why determinant data alone cannot certify that the chosen points generate the full lattice.
definitions: For independent generators P₁,…,P_r with symmetric height-pairing matrix G, the regulator is detG in the declared normalization.
Replacing the generator column by an integer matrix M changes the Gram matrix to G′=MᵀGM. A unimodular matrix has determinant±1.

result.name: A regulator is a Gram determinant tied to a generator basis
result.statement: detG′=(detM)²detG. A unimodular change preserves the regulator, while a finite-index sublattice of index m multiplies it by m². Linear dependence makes the Gram determinant zero.
result.proof: The determinant identity follows directly from multiplicativity of determinants and detMᵀ=detM. For a full-rank integer coordinate matrix, the index of the generated sublattice is |detM|, as can be proved by Smith form. Thus its squared covolume scales by the square of the index. Positive definiteness makes independent-vector Gram determinants positive. If the vectors are dependent, their coordinate matrix has a nontrivial kernel and so does their Gram matrix, forcing determinant zero.

example.setup: Take G=[[2,1],[1,3]], whose determinant is five.
example.calculation: The unimodular matrix M=[[1,1],[0,1]] gives G′=[[2,3],[3,7]], still with determinant five. Replacing the second generator by twice itself gives diag(1,2)ᵀGdiag(1,2)=[[2,2],[2,12]], whose determinant is twenty, four times five. The latter pair spans an index-two sublattice. A numerical determinant near twenty would therefore not by itself identify the full-lattice regulator.
example.conclusion: The regulator becomes an invariant with explicit basis and saturation conditions rather than a decimal detached from its generators.

entries.limits: An elliptic canonical-height computation additionally needs normalization, rigorous truncation bounds and a proof of independence. A Smith matrix from another complex does not certify those inputs. None of the historical decimal intervals is assumed verified here.
entries.extension: Given candidate points, certify the height matrix by intervals, bound its smallest eigenvalue away from zero, and prove saturation at each relevant prime before calling its determinant the full Mordell–Weil regulator.

entries.title: A real quadratic L-derivative is exactly the logarithm of a unit
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The Stark reframing supplied Q(√5), its golden unit and L′(0,χ). There is an elegant complete classical model: use the primitive even quadratic Dirichlet character modulo five. Hurwitz-zeta and gamma identities then evaluate its derivative exactly, without invoking an unproved general regulator theorem.
definitions: For Re(s)>1, L(s,χ₅)=5^(−s)Σ_(a=1)^4χ₅(a)ζ(s,a/5), then extend analytically using Hurwitz zeta.

result.name: A real quadratic L-derivative is exactly the logarithm of a unit
result.statement: L(0,χ₅)=0 and L′(0,χ₅)=logφ. The element φ is an algebraic unit of norm−1, satisfying φ²−φ−1=0. This is a precisely normalized regulator-sized logarithm, not a proof of every proposed Stark realization.
result.proof: Use the classical identities ζ(0,x)=1/2−x and ζ′(0,x)=logΓ(x)−(1/2)log(2π). The weighted constant and linear sums vanish, giving L(0)=0; thus differentiating5^(−s) contributes no extra term. The character sum is zero, so the log(2π) terms also cancel. Therefore L′(0)=log[Γ(1/5)Γ(4/5)/(Γ(2/5)Γ(3/5))]. Euler’s reflection formula turns the ratio into sin(2π/5)/sin(π/5)=2cos(π/5)=φ. The special-function identities are the explicit classical inputs; the cancellation and unit comparison are derived here. The conjugate unit is(1−√5)/2=−φ⁻¹, giving norm−1.

example.setup: Separate this character from unspecified ray-class data over Q(√5).
example.calculation: The displayed χ₅ is a character over Q of conductor five. It cuts out the real quadratic field, but is not by itself a complete choice of ray-class character over that field. Its derivative exponentiates to φ in the stated real embedding; the other embedding has negative value, and absolute logarithms or totally positive-unit conventions can introduce a factor two. Squaring φ gives a norm-one unit and doubles the logarithm.
example.conclusion: The recovered idea has an actual special-value identity and an exact algebraic unit certificate.

entries.limits: No general toric motivic class, mixed-signature Eisenstein cocycle or p-adic comparison is constructed. The universal claim of unconditional validity for all totally real or CM situations is not adopted.
entries.extension: Specify a genuine ray-class character, its infinity type and vanishing order, then compare a rigorously evaluated L-leading term with a candidate unit using a stated regulator map and norm relations.

entries.title: A heat supertrace equals an Euler index because nonzero modes pair
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The index tables have a rigorous finite analogue that explains the mechanism behind protection: a differential pairs nonzero even and odd modes, so their heat contributions cancel. An ordinary heat trace does not have this cancellation.
definitions: Take a two-term finite-dimensional real or complex Hilbert complex C⁰→ᵈC¹. Let D=d+d* on C⁰⊕C¹, graded even/odd.
The heat supertrace is Str(e^(−tD²))=Tr_(C⁰)e^(−td*d)−Tr_(C¹)e^(−tdd*).

result.name: A heat supertrace equals an Euler index because nonzero modes pair
result.statement: For every t≥0 in this finite-dimensional complex, Str(e^(−tD²))=dimkerd−dimcokerd=dimC⁰−dimC¹. More generally a finite complex has heat supertrace equal to its alternating cohomology dimension.
result.proof: The positive spectra of d*d and dd* agree including multiplicities: if d*d v=λv with λ>0, then dv≠0 and dd*(dv)=λdv, with inverse correspondence λ⁻¹d* on the eigenspaces. Hence e^(−tλ) cancels between the two graded traces. The remaining zero modes are kerd in degree zero and ker d*=cokerd in degree one. Rank-nullity gives their dimension difference dimC⁰−dimC¹. The same pairing on each degree proves the finite-complex statement, equivalently by decomposing into harmonic spaces and two-term exact pairs.

example.setup: Use d=[[1,−1],[0,0]] between two copies of R².
example.calculation: Both d*d and dd* have eigenvalues0,2. Each ordinary heat trace is1+e^(−2t), so the total ungraded trace is2+2e^(−2t), which changes with time. Their supertrace is zero for every t. The cohomology dimensions are one in each degree, also giving1−1=0. This explicitly demonstrates why the grading and the differential identity are part of the index theorem’s mechanism.
example.conclusion: A protected quantity can be constructed and checked, but its protection comes from a proved pairing of modes.

entries.limits: The finite theorem is not the Atiyah–Singer theorem for a differential operator on a manifold. Twists, boundary conditions and APS corrections require their own hypotheses. A generic residue trace has no reason to share this cancellation.
entries.extension: Construct a finite discretization that preserves d²=0 and grading exactly, then prove that its supertrace index matches a chosen topological cochain complex before taking any continuum limit.

entries.title: A theta heat equation and an elliptic transformation can be proved term by term
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The October tables included Jacobi forms, heat equations and modular period comparisons. The elementary theta series supplies a completely normalized case. It also shows why an index or coefficient bound cannot be copied between conventions without checking its transformation law.
definitions: For Imτ>0, set θ(τ,z)=Σ_(n∈Z)exp(πin²τ+2πinz). This uses q=exp(πiτ).
On compact subsets with Imτ bounded below, Gaussian decay dominates every fixed derivative in τ or z, allowing termwise differentiation.

result.name: A theta heat equation and an elliptic transformation can be proved term by term
result.statement: ∂_τθ=(1/(4πi))∂²_zθ. Also θ(τ,z+1)=θ(τ,z) and θ(τ,z+τ)=exp(−πiτ−2πiz)θ(τ,z). The last factor is the half-index convention for this theta function.
result.proof: Differentiating one term with respect to τ multiplies it byπin². Differentiating twice in z multiplies it by−4π²n²; division by4πi givesπin², proving the heat equation. Shifting z by one contributes exp(2πin)=1. For the τ shift, n²+2n=(n+1)²−1; reindexing n+1 extracts exp(−πiτ−2πiz) and leaves the original series. The convergent Gaussian bounds justify both the differentiations and the index shift, so these are identities of holomorphic functions on their stated domain.

example.calculation: At fixed τ the n=±1 terms are2qcos(2πz). Their z-second derivative divided by4πi is2πi qcos(2πz), exactly their τ derivative. But agreement of finitely many Fourier modes does not identify an unrestricted function: adding q^N changes none of the lower coefficients. A genuine Sturm-type certificate needs a specified finite-dimensional modular or Jacobi space, its weight, level, index and a correct theorem bounding vanishing.
example.conclusion: The exact transformation and heat identities are a solid base for a normalized modular-gauge comparison.

entries.title: An index does not determine Yukawa singular values
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The October program tried to link masses or Yukawa data to a protected index pushforward. Finite linear algebra gives a decisive constraint on any such bridge: an index can remain fixed while every nonzero singular value varies. A theorem relating them would need extra structure beyond index equality.
definitions: For a linear map Y:Cⁿ→Cᵐ, its finite Fredholm index is dimkerY−dimcokerY=n−m.
The singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of Y*Y and depend on the chosen Hermitian metrics. They are not determined by the index.

result.name: An index does not determine Yukawa singular values
result.statement: For Y_t:C→C² defined by z↦(tz,0), the index is−1 for every complex t, while its sole singular value is|t|. At t=0 the kernel and cokernel dimensions both jump, but their difference remains−1.
result.proof: If t≠0, the map is injective and its range has dimension one, so ker dimension is zero and coker dimension one. At zero, the kernel has dimension one and the cokernel dimension two. Both give index−1. Meanwhile Y_t*Y_t is the1×1 matrix|t|², proving the singular-value formula. The index equality also follows from rank-nullity for any finite map, regardless of its entries. Thus an index theorem at this level cannot recover a continuous scale such as|t| without another equation that restricts t.

example.setup: Compare t=1 with t=100 and with zero.
example.calculation: All three maps have the same index. Their singular values are1,100,0, and their operator norms have those same values. A proposed formula multiplying the singular value by a separately specified scale can consequently vary by a factor100 while every index datum remains unchanged. This is an exact family, not a numerical near-counterexample. Gauge or basis changes that are unitary preserve singular values, whereas arbitrary invertible basis changes need not.
example.conclusion: The distinction identifies the genuine mathematical burden of connecting a protected invariant to metric observables.

entries.limits: No physical mass convention is adopted from the recovered factor v/2, and no biological or particle prediction follows. A topological index may constrain zero modes or differences of dimensions without setting nonzero spectral scales.
entries.extension: State a metric or variational principle that restricts Y inside a fixed index class, then prove quantitative bounds on its singular values; only those added hypotheses can support a scale prediction.

entries.title: A Tor group requires modules and a resolution before it can model an obstruction
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The Higgs/torsor synthesis invoked Tor₁ without a specified resolution. A small exact model demonstrates what a derived tensor product detects: failure of a relation to remain injective after tensoring. This is meaningful homological mathematics but does not automatically identify a physical field.
definitions: Let R=k[x] over a field k and M=R/(x). A free resolution is0→R→ˣR→M→0.
Tor_i^R(M,N) is the i-th homology of a free resolution of M tensored with N. Ordinary tensor product is its degree-zero part.

result.name: A Tor group requires modules and a resolution before it can model an obstruction
result.statement: Tor₀^R(M,M)≅k and Tor₁^R(M,M)≅k, while higher Tor groups vanish for this resolution. By contrast Tor₁^R(R,M)=0 because R is free.
result.proof: Multiplication by x on R is injective, since the polynomial ring over a field is a domain; its cokernel is M, proving exactness of the resolution. Tensor with M. On M the element x acts as zero, so the resulting two-term complex is M→⁰M. Its kernel in degree one is M and its cokernel in degree zero is M, with no other terms. The one-term free resolution of R instead has no degree-one term, giving zero first Tor. The difference is structural: the relation x becomes zero after imposing x=0, leaving a degree-one class.

example.setup: Replace the second module by N=R/(x−1).
example.calculation: Multiplication by x acts as multiplication by one on N, so the tensored resolution is N→¹N, an isomorphism. Both its kernel and cokernel vanish. Thus Tor₁(M,N)=0 and M⊗N=0. The supports x=0 and x=1 do not meet, in contrast to the self-intersection example. This calculation supplies an explicit input-dependent obstruction, not a universal nonzero derived field.
example.conclusion: The categorical language now has an exact ring, modules, maps and homology certificate.

entries.limits: Nothing here identifies Tor₁ with a Higgs bundle, a particle mass or a determinant pushforward. Those interpretations would require a specified functor and a theorem preserving the relevant structures, not just matching notation.
entries.extension: For a declared intersection of algebraic subschemes, compute a Koszul resolution and determine when higher Tor measures nontransversality, then state precisely which geometric obstruction it represents.

entries.title: A Picard–Fuchs basis comparison is determined by values and derivatives at one regular point
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The period comparison returned genuinely mismatched certified leaves. A constant scale or symplectic mixing is a hypothesis to prove, not a consequence of the word period. The recovered second-order equation gives an exact local uniqueness test and a useful series certificate.
definitions: Consider(1−u²)a″−a/4=0 on a simply connected domain avoiding±1. A fundamental solution matrix records two solutions and their first derivatives.
For scalar solutions y₁,y₂, their Wronskian is W=y₁y₂′−y₁′y₂.

result.name: A Picard–Fuchs basis comparison is determined by values and derivatives at one regular point
result.statement: The Wronskian is constant. Any two fundamental matrices for the same equation differ by a constant invertible matrix. At u=0 the normalized solutions have expansions y₁=1+u²/8+3u⁴/128+⋯ and y₂=u+u³/24+5u⁵/384+⋯.

The constant is determined by the value-and-derivative matrices at any regular point. For a=Σc_nuⁿ, coefficient comparison yields c_(n+2)=[n(n−1)+1/4]c_n/[(n+2)(n+1)]. Substituting initial data(1,0) and(0,1) gives the displayed rational coefficients and W(0)=1.

entries.summary: The pre-geometric framework combined E₈, rank384 and φ(1680). These numbers can all be checked, but they count different mathematical objects. definitions: In R⁸ take roots of two kinds: vectors with two entries±1 and six zeros, and vectors with all entries±1/2 with an even number of minus signs.

result.name: The E₈ roots, its Lie dimension and the totient384 are different exact counts

entries.title: Semisimplicity kills ordinary extension classes
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The October audit correctly questioned using positive-degree Ext in a semisimple setting. The exact reason is elementary: every short exact sequence splits, and every object is projective. A deformation theory must therefore identify another complex or weaken semisimplicity.
definitions: An abelian category is semisimple here when every short exact sequence splits. In finite-dimensional vector spaces, every subspace has a complement.
Ext¹(C,A) classifies short exact sequences0→A→B→C→0 up to equivalence; higher Ext can be computed from projective resolutions when available.

result.name: Semisimplicity kills ordinary extension classes
result.statement: In a semisimple abelian category with the usual Ext construction, Extⁿ(C,A)=0 for n>0. For finite-dimensional vector spaces, a split extension is explicitly B≅A⊕C.
result.proof: Choose a section s:C→B of the surjection p:B→C. Then(a,c)↦i(a)+s(c) is an isomorphism A⊕C→B: injectivity follows after applying p, and surjectivity follows by subtracting s(p(b)) from b. Hence every extension represents the zero class in Ext¹. More generally, given an epimorphism and a map from any object, a splitting of the epimorphism lifts that map; therefore every object is projective. A resolution concentrated in degree zero computes all higher Ext as zero. This is a theorem about this specific derived functor, not every cohomology assigned to a tensor category.

example.setup: Compare vector spaces with modules over the dual numbers k[ε]/(ε²).
example.calculation: In the latter category the sequence0→k→k[ε]/(ε²)→k→0, where the first map sends1 to ε, does not split as a module sequence. A hypothetical lift of1 from the quotient would be1+cε, but multiplication by ε sends it to ε≠0, whereas ε acts as zero on k. Thus nontrivial extensions arise once the semisimple hypothesis is removed.
example.conclusion: The framework must select an obstruction theory that survives its own assumptions, rather than assigning nonzero Ext classes where they are forced to vanish.

entries.limits: Davydov–Yetter, Hochschild and other deformation cohomologies have their own definitions; this argument does not identify them or claim they all vanish. A software field called cohomology does not fix which functor is intended.
entries.extension: Specify the tensor-deformation cochain complex and prove that its differential squares to zero, then compute a low-degree example before interpreting it as geometric curvature.

entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The dashboard selected high entropy and low maximal displacement, then inserted its selection into a coupling predictor. The optimization itself has a precise finite theory. definitions: For pairs(d,H), smaller d and larger H are preferred. A point is dominated if another has no larger d and no smaller H, with at least one strict improvement.

entries.title: Heat residues follow from a Mellin transform and need not be integer indices
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The Global Residue Index proposal combined spectral residues, complex residues and integer indices. A circle Laplacian gives a complete countercheck and a positive calculation: its heat leading term determines a zeta residue that varies continuously with the circle length.
definitions: On a circle of circumference L, remove the zero mode from −d²/dx². The nonzero eigenvalues are(2πn/L)²,n∈Z minus{0}.

entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The recovered identity[d,π₊]ω=∫Ω_L∧ω requires a type check before a geometric interpretation. With ordinary exterior derivative and a curvature two-form, its sides have different degrees. A closed-product-fiber calculation supplies the correct elementary comparison.
definitions: Let π:B×F→B with F a closed oriented m-manifold. Write horizontal forms before vertical forms and defineπ! by integrating the vertical top-degree coefficient.

result.name: Fiber integration commutes with d on closed product fibers in a fixed convention

entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The recovered formula used half the standard logarithmic correction in the Bloch–Wigner function. The normalized function has a useful exact functional relation. Adding it to log|z| gives a legitimate real observable, but generally only one constraint on a two-dimensional variable.
definitions: On compatible branches away from0 and1 use D(z)=ImLi₂(z)+log|z|Arg(1−z), extended as the standard single-valued Bloch–Wigner function.

result.name: The Bloch–Wigner correction has coefficient one, and a scalar residue leaves a level curve
result.statement: The normalized function satisfies D(1−z)=−D(z). A coefficient1/2 in its correction fails this relation in general. Near any real x∈(0,1), the equation R(z)=logx defines a local real one-dimensional level curve, rather than uniquely determining z.

Adding the two full correction terms cancels it, proving antisymmetry on compatible branches and then by continuation. Half corrections leave half the uncanceled expression. Along the real interval R(x)=logx, so its derivative in the real direction is1/x≠0. The real implicit-function theorem therefore gives a smooth one-dimensional local level set of R in the complex plane.

entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The operator report asserted a compact trace-class but non-Hilbert–Schmidt limit. Under the standard definitions this is impossible. definitions: For a compact operator A on a Hilbert space, let s_n(A)≥0 be its singular values. Trace class meansΣs_n<∞; Hilbert–Schmidt meansΣs_n²<∞.

result.name: Trace class is contained in Hilbert–Schmidt, and strong convergence alone preserves neither
result.statement: Every trace-class operator is Hilbert–Schmidt, with||A||_HS≤||A||₁. Compactness does not imply either summability condition. A strong limit of finite-rank operators need not even be compact.
result.proof: For any finite nonnegative sequence,Σs_n²≤(Σs_n)²; monotone limits give the norm inequality when the trace norm is finite. For diagonal operators on ℓ², compactness is equivalent to diagonal entries tending to zero, and the two ideal conditions reduce to the displayed scalar series. Thus diag(1/n) is Hilbert–Schmidt but not trace class, while diag(1/√n) is compact but not Hilbert–Schmidt. Coordinate projections P_N have finite rank and converge strongly to identity because the ℓ² tail of every fixed vector tends to zero. Identity is not compact on an infinite-dimensional space, since its image of the orthonormal unit vectors has no norm-convergent subsequence.

definitions: For X≥2 set λ_X(t)=Σ_(p≤X)(logp)/(1+p)[2cos(tlogp)−2]+t/2.

entries.title: The sine quotient has an exact parity integral and a finite quadrature certificate
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The parity integral is one of the clearest exact mathematics problems recovered in October. Its apparent endpoint singularities are removable for integer a, and a finite trigonometric expansion proves both the integral and a useful sampling theorem.
definitions: For a positive integer a define I(a)=∫₀^(aπ)sinx/sin(x/a)dx, interpreted by continuous endpoint limits.
Substitute x=aθ to get I(a)=a∫₀πU_(a−1)(cosθ)dθ, where U_(a−1)(cosθ)=sin(aθ)/sinθ.

result.name: The sine quotient has an exact parity integral and a finite quadrature certificate
result.statement: I(a)=aπ for odd a and zero for even a. For odd a=2m+1, the N-point midpoint rule in θ is exact whenever m<N. For even a its symmetric midpoint sum is zero for every N.
result.proof: For odd a=2m+1, the quotient equals1+2Σ_(k=1)^mcos(2kθ); for even a=2m it equals2Σ_(k=1)^mcos((2k−1)θ). Both follow from a finite geometric sum of complex exponentials. Integrating each nonconstant integer cosine over[0,π] gives zero, leavingπ only in the odd case. The expansion also removes the endpoint singularities. At midpoint nodes θ_j=(j+1/2)π/N, the sum of cos(2kθ_j) vanishes when1≤k<N, by a geometric sum. Every odd-frequency cosine sum vanishes by pairing θ_j withπ−θ_j, proving the even case.

example.setup: Take a=5 and N=3.
example.calculation: The quotient is1+2cos2θ+2cos4θ. Both cosine sums vanish at the three midpoint nodes, so the midpoint integral equalsπ and I(5)=5π exactly. If each sampled quotient value has absolute error at mostδ, the propagated integration error is at most aπδ, because the positive quadrature weights sum to aπ. This is a mathematical error bound; hardware specifications alone do not imply a particular δ.
example.conclusion: The exact parity identity and its discrete certificate follow from the same finite Fourier structure.

entries.limits: The theorem concerns positive integer a. Noninteger values may introduce interior poles and require a different integration prescription. No energy conversion, superconductivity or self-calibration claim follows from the integral identity.

entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The exact input is Ψ=∫₀^(π/4)log[(1+x²)sin¹⁰x]dx. Separating its logarithms produces a complete evaluation with a familiar special constant, and prevents later large integer factors from obscuring the original expression.
definitions: Let a=π/4 and G=Σ_(n≥0)(−1)^n/(2n+1)², Catalan’s constant.

result.name: The logarithmic sine integral separates into an elementary term and Catalan’s constant
result.statement: Ψ=a log(1+a²)−2a+2arctana−10a log2−5G, with a=π/4.
result.proof: An elementary primitive is∫log(1+x²)dx=xlog(1+x²)−2x+2arctanx, verified by differentiation. For the sine term use the Abel-regularized Fourier expansion log(2sinx)=−Σ_(n≥1)cos(2nx)/n on(0,π). Integrating its convergent radial regularizations from0 to a and taking the limit gives∫₀ᵃlogsinx dx=−a log2−(1/2)Σ_(n≥1)sin(2na)/n². At a=π/4, the sine values cycle1,0,−1,0, so this sum is G. Multiplying by ten and adding the elementary part gives the formula. Absolute convergence of the integrated1/n² series makes its final evaluation unambiguous.

example.calculation: Truncating G after N odd-denominator terms has alternating-series error at most1/(2N+1)². Its contribution to Ψ is at most5/(2N+1)². Bounds forπ, logarithms and arctangent can then be propagated separately. Uniform convergence applies on the remaining compact interval, while the integral of|logx| over(0,ε) tends to zero. The integrated Fourier series is absolutely summable, so its final Catalan specialization is independent of the approach.

entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The recovered input is I=∫₀¹[(sin(log√t−π/4)+cos(π/4−log√t))/(logπ·log(t²))]⁴dt. Its numerator simplifies before any integration. A Laplace transform and three integrations by parts then verify the reported closed form exactly.

Define K(a)=∫₀∞e^(−av)sin⁴v/v⁴ dv for a>0. The sine quotient tends to one at zero and exponential decay controls infinity.

result.name: The recovered fourth-power logarithmic integral has an exact elementary evaluation
result.proof: The substitution gives I=K(2)/[32(logπ)⁴]. Use8sin⁴v=3−4cos2v+cos4v and set H(v)=e^(−av)(3−4cos2v+cos4v). H and its first three derivatives vanish at zero, while they decay at infinity. Applying the elementary Frullani identity∫₀∞(e^(−λv)−e^(−μv))/v dv=log(μ/λ), valid for positive real parts with continuous logarithm, yields K(a)=(1/48)Re[3a³loga−4(a−2i)³log(a−2i)+(a−4i)³log(a−4i)]. entries.title: Cyclotomic trace orthogonality fixes the coefficient p, not p+1
entries.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
entries.summary: The retrieved cyclotomic expression used a coefficient p+1 and reported30/13 in a character setting. Summing the actual embeddings gives an exact trace identity and a useful integrality test, while leaving the unrecovered original coefficient data unspecified.
definitions: Let p be prime, ζ=exp(2πi/p), and X=Σ_(k=0)^(p−1)a_kζ^k. For the trace formula first allow a_k∈Q.

result.name: Cyclotomic trace orthogonality fixes the coefficient p, not p+1
result.statement: Tr_(Q(ζ)/Q)(X²)=pC₀−A². If all a_k are integers, this trace is an integer. The same integrality holds for every algebraic-integer X, including ordinary finite-group character values contained in this field.
result.proof: The embedding sumΣ_(r=1)^(p−1)ζ^(rm) is p−1 if p divides m and−1 otherwise: include the r=0 term and use a geometric series. Expand X² and apply this sum to every pair(k,ℓ). Congruence-zero pairs contribute(p−1)C₀, and the other pairs contribute−(A²−C₀), giving pC₀−A². For integral coefficients the formula is visibly integral. More generally the field trace of an algebraic integer is a rational algebraic integer, hence an ordinary integer. Thus a noninteger30/13 cannot be that trace without changing the object or its normalization.

example.setup: Take p=5 and X=ζ+ζ⁻¹.

example.conclusion: The trace is now an explicit finite embedding sum with a sharp algebraic consistency check.

entries.status: Classical or newly chosen explicit model developed with proof; historical conjectures delimited
entries.summary: The recovered integral was described as lacking an elementary closed form. Its asymmetry disappears under x↦−x, leaving the classical Fourier transform of a quartic rational function. The resulting formula is exact for every real modulation parameter.
definitions: Let a∈R and I(a)=∫R cos²(ax)/[(1+ix²)(1+4^x)(1−ix²)]dx.
Write w(x)=1/(1+4^x); then w(x)+w(−x)=1.

result.name: Parity reduction and quartic transform
result.proof: The conjugate factors multiply to1+x⁴. The remaining factor f(x)=cos²(ax)/(1+x⁴) is even and integrable. Substitution x↦−x gives I=∫f(x)w(−x)dx, so adding yields2I=∫f. Now cos²(ax)=(1+cos2ax)/2. For b>0 close the contour for e^(ibz)/(1+z⁴) in the upper half-plane; the poles are e^(i π/4) and e^(3i π/4), with residues e^(ibz)/(4z³). Their sum, multiplied by2π i, is F(b)=π e^(−b/√2)[cos(b/√2)+sin(b/√2)]/√2. The large arc vanishes by the exponential factor and quartic denominator; b=0 follows directly or by dominated convergence. Evenness supplies F(−b)=F(b). Therefore I=(F(0)+F(2a))/4, proving the formula. Every exchange is justified by domination with1/(1+x⁴).

entries.title: A positive kernel is not necessarily positive definite
entries.status: Classical or newly chosen explicit model developed with proof; historical conjectures delimited
entries.summary: The recovered kernel discussion moved from positive integrands to kernel methods and a conjectured spectral decay. A covariance or reproducing kernel must satisfy all finite Gram-matrix inequalities, a much stronger condition than having positive values.
definitions: A Hermitian kernel k(x, y) is positive definite if Σ overline c_i c_j k(x_i, x_j)≥0 for every finite point set and coefficients.

result.name: An exact quartic Gram counterexample
result.statement: The pointwise positive even function f(t)=1/(1+t⁴) is not positive definite on R. Its Gram matrix at points−1/2,0,1/2 has negative determinant−157/1156.
result.proof: At adjacent separation1/2, f=16/17; at separation1, f=1/2. The Gram matrix is[[1, a, b],[a,1, a],[b, a,1]] witha=16/17, b=1/2. Expanding its determinant gives(1−b)(1+b−2a²). Here1+b−2a²=3/2−512/289=−157/578, so the determinant is−157/1156. A positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix has nonnegative determinant, proving failure. An even more immediate obstruction affects the original real asymmetric logistic factor: a translation kernel using it is not even, hence not Hermitian. On the other hand the quartic Fourier transform F(b)=∫e^(ibx)/(1+x⁴)dx is positive definite as a function of b: the Gram quadratic form equals∫|Σ c_j e^(ib_jx)|²/(1+x⁴)dx≥0. The response and its Fourier transform therefore play different roles.

Thus pointwise nonnegativity is neither necessary nor sufficient for positive definiteness. A valid covariance can have negative correlations, whereas a positive-valued response can fail the covariance test.

definitions: Let τ:T³→S² be smooth, w∈L²(T³) nonnegative, and ρ_r∈L¹(R³) nonnegative with total mass one and support |h|≤2r. Evaluate torus functions periodically for h∈R³.

result.name: Exact weighted FTC–Jensen bound
result.statement: A(r)≤4r²∫||∇τ(y)||²J_r(y)dy, where J_r(y)=ess sup_(s∈[0,1])∫w(y−sh)w(y+(1−s)h)ρ_r(h)dh. If J_r≤C_int w² almost everywhere for a finite C_int>0, then ∫w²||∇τ||²≥A(r)/(4r²C_int).
result.proof: For unit vectorsu, v,1−(u·v)²=(1−u·v)(1+u·v)≤2(1−u·v)=||u−v||². Along the straight torus displacementh, the fundamental theorem gives τ(x+h)−τ(x)=∫₀¹∇τ(x+sh)h ds. Jensen bounds its squared norm by|h|²∫₀¹||∇τ(x+sh)||²ds. Insert this in A, use|h|²≤4r², and change variablesy=x+sh. Tonelli applies because all terms are nonnegative. The resultingh-integral at fixeds, yis bounded by J_r(y); integratingsgives the claimed inequality. The final lower bound follows only after inserting J_r≤C_int w². The alternative assumption J_r≤C_int w instead yields a lower bound for ∫w||∇τ||²; these are different hypotheses. If w vanishes where J_r is positive, no finite factor exists. Essential suprema avoid dependence on representatives in the interpolation parameter.

entries.title: A conditional proof chain is not a verified closure
entries.status: Classical or newly chosen explicit model developed with proof; historical conjectures delimited
entries.summary: The recovered Leanfiles retainedaxioms and anadmitat the production-versus-dissipation step, while earlier output claimed compilation and completion. A precise logical model distinguishes a valid conditional theorem from evidence that its analytic hypotheses hold. The same distinction applies to a certifier that inserts its target matrix.
definitions: Suppose statements P, Q, Rstand for disorder, intermittency and transverse regeneration, and Gfor global regularity.
A theorem deriving Gfrom assumptions P, Q, Rproves(P∧Q∧R)⇒G; it does not prove the antecedent.

result.name: Countermodel test for an alleged unconditional conclusion
result.statement: The implication(P∧Q∧R)⇒Gcan be true even when Gis false, because the antecedent may be false. Likewise verifying eigenvalues of a hard-coded matrix certifies that matrix, not its provenance from an unavailable source operator.
result.proof: Use a Boolean model with P=false, Q=true, R=true, G=false. The conjunction is false, and material implication fromfalseis true. Thus the conditional theorem can be logically valid in a model where Gfails, proving that unconditional Gdoes not follow from that implication alone. In a proof assistant, the theorem’s dependency list records the assumed constants or axioms used; compilation checks the derivation relative to them. Replacing a missing analytic estimate by an axiom moves it into the assumptions rather than solving it. For matrix certification, the same separation is algebraic:if M₂=[[5/8,631/25000],[0,5/8]]is declared, its characteristic polynomial is(t−5/8)²and its nilpotent residual is square-zero.
